555.t: Meeting Randy Weston and the Little Niles album
555.s: Randy met her at Birdland, had her write the lead sheets of Little Niles into an album with Johnny Griffin and Ray Copeland, and she has written nearly all his multi-horn albums.
555.q: I was playing with Dizzy – I guess Birdland. I came out and did my usual thing. He stayed over and met me when I finished the gig. He said, “I have to meet her.” We just hit it off right away.

555.s: They hear her 1956 arrangement of Randy Weston's Little Niles, featuring bass, with a Monk flavor.
555.q: Yeah, but I didn’t know. I forgot. The other one is more ballad and it’s easier.

555.t: Randy Weston's ballad featuring her, recorded in Montreal
555.s: They play an untitled waltz-time ballad with her solo, written for her; the record was made with Montreal strings.
555.q: [while the music plays] So that – don’t stop it, but that’s about all that I can say, that I’m featured on it. That little bit. But it’s nice.

555.t: Little Niles with strings, from Earth Birth
555.s: They hear the new strings version; Liston says horns and strings play the same parts, and Randy only tells her choruses and string entrances.
555.q: The horn parts and the string parts are the same. The horns played what the strings are playing there.

555.s: They listen to the 1973 version, which Bryant hears as East Indian and African, and note Randy reuses Little Niles and Pam's Waltz.
555.q: Today they could program it much better than it was on that, but you could hear it, but if they were to do it now . . .

555.t: Hi-Fly in 1973 and 1996 versions; writing for strings
555.s: They compare two Hi-Fly arrangements, Liston says she has written strings as long as horns, and Randy only tells her who solos where.
555.q: He doesn’t say nothing about the soloing and all that. He wanted it long, and he said, “This chorus I’ll take by myself. This chorus you can do some backgrounds or something.”

667.t: The new 'East of Suez' arrangement for Concord
667.s: Carl Jefferson asks for 'East of Suez' for a Concord album; the song's origin as a Lou Stein tune for Ventura.
667.ch: Studio notes, hits and old friends
667.q: That was actually a Lou Stein tune that he had written for Charlie and Charlie did it with Buddy Stewart and Kai Winding. And it was recorded that way the first time, but then when we joined the band he wanted us to do it naturally, because it was a good record for him, a big record. So that’s how…

213.t: LP side length, High Fly and the 6/8 tunes
213.s: He explains LP timing, putting High Fly first on side two as a hedge, and Randy Weston's and Cannonball's 6/8 numbers.
213.q: Oh yeah. But nevertheless I just felt this was such a characteristic of the guy, and we did the same thing, because if you can remember back before the CD, there was side one and there was side two. And since one might be marked one, your second most important spot on an LP, and for audience…

468.t: Last-minute solo bass on Night Train and Little Sunflower
468.s: He put off arranging his solo bass feature, devised Night Train in twenty minutes and did three takes.
468.q: Yeah. Every time I think about how I did it I get tired. Because I did the same thing on the new album as I did on “Getting To It.” The producer said, “Well you know why don’t you feature yourself on something, you know, just unaccompanied bass?” I said well sometimes — this is not a good habit —…

947.t: 'Cast Your Fate to the Wind' and Vince Guaraldi
947.s: They discuss versions of 'Cast Your Fate to the Wind', Sounds Orchestral, Guaraldi's original and the key of A flat.
947.q: Well if I may, because I remember this and was alive then. It was way before your time, but whatever it was, ’64 maybe, the hit version was this orchestral thing you’re referring to. A nameless, you know a studio orchestra that they called Sounds Orchestral. That was the hit. To me, you’re right,…

110.t: Origin of Blue Rondo a la Turk and Columbia's A-side decision
110.s: He heard a 9/8 street rhythm in Turkey, wrote Blue Rondo, and Columbia chose Take Five as the A side.
110.q: I was on my way to a radio station to be interviewed in Turkey. I was walking through the streets. There were street musicians playing in 9/8. [Brubeck sings a 9/8 rhythmic pattern.] Like that. So when I got to the radio station, there was a wonderful musician named June [ ], a friend of Gunther…
